1387.title: The spire at Pandharpur
1387.hook: the walk is over, the line to the god stretches out of sight, and some pilgrims bow to the temple's spire and turn for home
1387.carry: even a bow to the spire is darshan
1387.tomorrow: how do you beat a demon who hides under water?
1387.howItsDone: At Pandharpur, Varkaris bathe in the Chandrabhaga, wait for darshan of Vitthal, where pilgrims may touch his feet, or bow to the temple's pinnacle from outside, then return home.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti belongs to everyone, even at the grindstone: Janabai singing before dawn, and Vitthal taking the handle.
screen: `MAHARASHTRA'S VARKARI.`

segments.voice: After all those days of walking, the town comes into view: Pandharpur, on the bank of the river. The singing gets louder, not softer. Then the walkers see the line to stand before Vitthal. It winds through the streets and out of sight. Some will wait in it for many hours. And some, the story of the road says, walk down to the river, bathe, look up at the temple's spire, bow, and turn for home, content. So was the whole walk wasted, for the ones who never reach his feet?
screen: `PANDHARPUR COMES INTO VIEW.` → `A LINE OUT OF SIGHT.` → `A BOW TO THE SPIRE.`

segments.voice: The river at Pandharpur is the Bhima, and here Varkaris call it the Chandrabhaga, because, tradition says, it bends like a crescent moon. Pilgrims bathe in it first. On the holy day itself, the Ekadashi, the crowd reaches its peak. Inside the temple, Vitthal stands on his brick, hands on hips, the way Pundalik left him, and pilgrims are allowed close enough to lay their heads on his feet. A child running to a mother doesn't stop at arm's length. But the line is long, and not everyone reaches the feet. So Varkari tradition holds that seeing the kalas, the temple's pinnacle, from outside is darshan too. Darshan is one of the plainest acts of Hindu worship: you go to see God, and, just as much, to be seen by God. And in the Varkari songs, Vitthal is the one who waits: he stood on that brick for Pundalik and never left. Many teachers read it this way: a God who is waiting is already looking at you, whether you're at his feet or on the riverbank. Then the walkers go home, to fields and shops and kitchens, until the next wari. And it's why, at any temple, someone who can't manage the line may fold their hands toward the spire from outside, and mean it. The walk wasn't wasted. They were seen.
screen: `A BATH IN THE CHANDRABHAGA` · `A HEAD ON VITTHAL'S FEET` · `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN` · `THE SPIRE COUNTS TOO`

segments.voice: Find one image that's holy to you, a picture of a god on a shelf, a temple you love, or just the sky through a window, and look at it the way pilgrims look up at the spire: steadily, hands folded if you like. For a few breaths, let yourself be looked at back. If you don't pray, rest your eyes on something you love and let seeing it from where you are be enough.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who reach Pandharpur, bow at Vitthal's feet or to his spire, and go home until the next wari. Today's word.

1388.title: The lake that became Kashmir
1388.hook: before the valley there was a lake, and in the lake a demon who could not be caught while he stayed in the water
1388.carry: the earth is holy; we ask her pardon
1388.tomorrow: a poet sets out to tell of kings. what's the first rule he sets?
1388.howItsDone: Kashmiri Hindus tell the story of Satisar, the lake drained so the demon Jalodbhava could be defeated, as the beginning of the valley, and honor its springs and rivers as sacred.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, even a bow to the spire is darshan: the Varkari road ended at Pandharpur, and the walkers went home.
screen: `MAHARASHTRA'S VARKARI.`

segments.voice: Before there was a valley, the old book says, there was a lake. Mountains all around, and water filling the space between them, still and deep. And in that water lived a demon. As long as he stayed in the lake, nobody could touch him; he came out to raid the lands nearby and slipped back under the surface. The gods couldn't reach him. So how do you defeat someone who hides in the water? You take away the water, and what's left is the ground a whole people will call holy.
screen: `A LAKE BETWEEN MOUNTAINS.` → `A DEMON HIDING IN THE WATER.` → `TAKE AWAY THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The book is the Nilamata Purana, a Sanskrit text of Kashmir, and here it is in paraphrase. The lake was called Satisar, the lake of Sati, the goddess. The demon in it was Jalodbhava. He couldn't be killed in his element, so the sage Kashyapa went to the gods and asked for help. Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma came. The mountain wall was opened, the water drained away, and the demon, left on dry ground, was struck down. What was left behind was a green valley, and people came to live in it. Tradition links Kashmir's name with Kashyapa, the sage who asked. Now the teaching. For Kashmiri Hindus, the valley isn't just land. Its floor was once the goddess's lake, and the rivers and springs that remained are holy, places families still go to bathe and pray. That's an old Hindu instinct: the earth itself is sacred. The Earth is honored as a goddess, Bhudevi, Mother Earth, and many Hindus, on waking, touch the floor before they step on it and say a short Sanskrit verse asking her to forgive them for touching her with their feet. Before a house is built, families hold a bhoomi puja, a worship of the ground, before the digging starts. So a story about one valley says out loud what every Hindu morning says quietly: the ground under you is holy. This week, more from the valley, starting from the lake.
screen: `THE LAKE OF SATI` · `KASHYAPA ASKS, THE LAKE DRAINS` · `A HOLY VALLEY` · `THE EARTH IS A GODDESS`

segments.voice: Before you get up from where you're sitting, lower one hand and touch the floor, the way many Hindus do on waking, then bring that hand to your forehead or your heart. Let it be a small sorry and thank you to the ground that holds you all day. If you know the morning verse to Mother Earth, say it; if you don't pray, let the touch itself be your thanks.
Kashmir. The valley that, the Nilamata Purana says, was once the lake of Sati, drained when the sage Kashyapa asked the gods for help. Today's word.

segments.voice: Hold on to this: the earth is holy; we ask her pardon. A valley began, the story says, as a goddess's lake. Until tomorrow.

1389.title: Kalhana's river of kings
1389.hook: a poet sits down to write the story of his valley's kings, and the first rule he sets himself is to be like a judge
1389.carry: see it straight, free of raga and dvesha
1389.tomorrow: why does crying at a sad play leave you lighter?
1389.howItsDone: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is read in Sanskrit and in translation as the chronicle of Kashmir's kings; Kashmiri Hindus treasure it as the valley's own story, beginning from the lake of Satisar.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the earth is holy; we ask her pardon: the earth is holy; we ask her pardon began as Sati's lake, drained at the sage Kashyapa's asking.
screen: `THE EARTH IS HOLY; WE ASK HER PARDON.`

segments.voice: A poet in Kashmir has a big job ahead of him. He's going to tell the story of the valley's kings, the good and the cruel, the wise and the foolish, in Sanskrit verse. Before he starts, he sets himself a rule. A poet who tells the past, he says, deserves praise only if his words are like a judge's: free of love and free of hate. No flattery for a patron. No revenge on an enemy. The poet's name is Kalhana. His book is the Rajatarangini, the river of kings.
screen: `A POET AND A VALLEY OF KINGS.` → `LIKE A JUDGE.` → `THE RIVER OF KINGS.`

segments.voice: Kalhana's book opens with verses honoring Shiva, then turns to the valley and tells yesterday's lake again: the water of Satisar drained and the land made ready for people. From there it runs on, king after king, like a river. That's the picture in the title: kings rising and passing like waves on moving water. Kalhana doesn't pretend the kings were all heroes. He tells of greed and plots and wasted lives alongside generosity and good rule. That's what his rule about the judge is for. If you love one side or hate another, you bend the story. That pair has a name in Hindu teaching: raga and dvesha, liking and loathing. The Bhagavad Gita says the two sit waiting in everything the senses meet, and warns: don't fall under their sway. Kalhana carries that teaching to his writing desk. He also says he read older chronicles and records and pieced them together. Then comes something a reader might not look for in a history. Kalhana says the mood he wants the whole work to leave behind is calm: in the language of Indian poetics, the rasa of shanta, peace. Why calm, for a story full of kings? Because if you watch power rise and fall long enough, you stop gripping it. The waves come and go. The river keeps moving. And the rule holds for anyone telling a story about people they know: a fight between friends, a family quarrel. Before you tell it, notice where liking or loathing is leaning on the words.
screen: `A HISTORY THAT OPENS WITH SHIVA` · `TOLD LIKE A JUDGE` · `RAGA AND DVESHA: LIKING, LOATHING` · `ITS MOOD IS CALM`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one recent disagreement in a single plain sentence, as Kalhana would: what happened, and what each person did, without a word of praise or blame. Read it back and cross out any word where liking or loathing crept in. Then let it go, like a wave on moving water.
Kashmir. The valley whose kings Kalhana set down in the Rajatarangini, the river of kings, told like a judge and meant to leave the reader calm. Today's word.
screen: `KASHMIR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Take this with you: see it straight, free of raga and dvesha. Even a history of kings, here, is meant to leave you calm. More from the valley tomorrow.

1390.title: Why a sad play feels good
1390.hook: a theater audience weeps at a tragedy and walks out into the night strangely at peace, and a Kashmiri teacher asks why
1390.carry: rasa: a taste of the awareness called Shiva
1390.tomorrow: she loves him, he's standing right there, and she feels nothing. why?
1390.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism and of Indian poetics read Abhinavagupta's writings with teachers, and his account of rasa is still taught to students of classical dance, music and theater.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, see it straight, free of raga and dvesha: Kalhana's river of kings, told like a judge.
screen: `KASHMIR.`

segments.voice: On stage, a grieving lover cries out, and down in the seats people are wiping their eyes. Then the play ends, the lamps go out, and they walk home under the stars, talking quietly, somehow lighter than when they came. Nobody died in their house tonight. They wept anyway, and it did them good. Why does a sad story feel like a gift? A teacher in Kashmir thought hard about that question, and his answer reached all the way to Shiva. His name is Abhinavagupta.
screen: `TEARS IN THE THEATER.` → `LIGHTER ON THE WAY HOME.` → `ABHINAVAGUPTA ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Abhinavagupta is remembered as a teacher who wrote about two things that might seem far apart: the art of theater and poetry, and the way to Shiva. In his tradition they turn out to be close. Start with the theater. Indian poetics speaks of rasa, the taste of a work of art. In a tragedy there's real sorrow in the story, but it isn't your private sorrow. You don't have to fix anything or protect anyone. So the feeling comes to you loosened from your own small worries, and you can savor it, the way you savor a flavor. That's rasa. In that moment, Abhinavagupta explained, the viewer's little self, my problems, my plans, steps aside, and what's left is a kind of open, tasting awareness, with a quality of rest and wonder. Then he made the bold link. If a play can briefly lift us into wide, delighted awareness, that awareness isn't something the play adds. It was there all along. And in his Shaiva teaching, that wide awareness is what Shiva is. The theater gives a glimpse, borrowed, for an evening. The path is about seeing it without the borrowing. Tradition adds an ending to his own story: one day he walked into a cave with his disciples, chanting, and was not seen again. Kalhana's river flowed toward calm. Abhinavagupta's road runs through a theater, to the same quiet.
screen: `THEATER AND SHIVA, TOGETHER` · `RASA: THE TASTE OF ART` · `THE SMALL SELF STEPS ASIDE` · `THE AWARENESS WAS ALWAYS THERE`

segments.voice: Let a little of the feeling from a song, a film or a story that once moved you return. Then gently notice what's noticing it: the feeling comes and goes, but something is aware of it the whole time, wide and quiet. Rest there, in the tasting, without needing the feeling to stay.
Kashmir. The valley where Abhinavagupta taught that the taste of a play, the rasa, is a glimpse of the wide awareness his tradition calls Shiva. Today's word.
screen: `KASHMIR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: rasa, a taste of the awareness called Shiva. The quiet behind every play was there all along. Same time tomorrow.

1391.title: The beloved in the room
1391.hook: a woman has longed for a man she's only heard described; he stands in front of her, and nothing happens, until someone says, that's him
1391.carry: pratyabhijna: recognize the Shiva already here
1391.tomorrow: why would anyone carry rice pudding to a spring?
1391.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism study Utpaladeva's teaching on recognition with a teacher, and his hymns to Shiva are read and recited as devotion.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa: a taste of the awareness called Shiva. Tears at a play, and the quiet doing the tasting.
screen: `RASA: A TASTE OF THE AWARENESS CALLED SHIVA.`

segments.voice: A young woman has fallen in love with a man she's never met. She's only heard about him: how kind he is, how he speaks, what he's done. She thinks about him all the time. Then one day he comes to her house and stands right in front of her. And she feels nothing much; he's just a visitor. Until someone at her side leans over and says: that's him. Everything changes, though not one thing in the room has moved. A teacher in Kashmir used that story to explain what he meant by recognition.
screen: `IN LOVE WITH SOMEONE UNMET.` → `HE STANDS IN FRONT OF HER.` → `THAT'S HIM.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Utpaladeva, a Shaiva thinker of Kashmir, and the story comes, in paraphrase, from his work on recognition. That word is the key: pratyabhijna. Not finding something new. Recognizing what's already in front of you. In his teaching, Shiva isn't far off. Shiva is the very awareness you're living in, the one who sees and knows, right now. So the problem was never that God is missing. It's like the woman in the story: her beloved is standing in the room, and she's still longing, because she hasn't recognized him. Nothing needs to be brought in. Something needs to be seen. Look at what makes the difference: someone at her side who says, that's him. In Utpaladeva's tradition, that's the role of a teacher and of teaching. The teacher doesn't hand you a new self. The teacher points. Notice the joy, too. She doesn't get a lecture on who he is. The recognition itself is the delight. And Utpaladeva also wrote hymns to Shiva, full of longing and tenderness, and the two belong together: the more you see that he's here, the more there is to sing about. The week's Kashmir has been building this way: a valley drained so a hidden thing could be seen, a history told without bending, a theater where the small self steps aside, and now a woman who simply recognizes who's in the room.

segments.voice: A bowl of rice pudding, cooked slowly in milk, carried in two hands down a path under tall trees. At the end of the path there's a spring, and in the middle of the spring, a small shrine. People bend at the edge of the water and offer the pudding, kheer, and milk, and flowers. Then they do something you might not expect at a temple. They look down, carefully, at the color of the water. Why bring pudding to a goddess, and why read her water?

segments.voice: The shrine stands in a village called Tulmul, not far from Srinagar. The goddess there is called Ragnya, or Maharagnya, a form of the Mother. She also goes by a homelier name: Kheer Bhawani, Bhawani of the rice pudding, because of what her devotees bring her. Bhawani is a name of the Goddess, the wife of Shiva, so the name holds the kitchen and the heavens together. That's the teaching inside the name. Many Hindus come to the Goddess as Ma, Mother, and you bring a mother food from your own kitchen. The offering is called naivedya. Once she has received it, it comes back as prasad, her blessing, to be eaten. It's why so many Hindu homes set the first portion aside for God before anyone eats. The shrine sits in the water, and the water matters too. Tradition says the spring changes color: pilgrims say clear, light shades are a good sign, and dark shades have been read as a warning of hard times for the valley. Some take that as a plain wonder; others hear a community that keeps watching the same water together, year after year. The goddess of Tulmul is especially dear to Kashmiri Pandits, the Hindu community of the valley. Her festival day is kept as a homecoming, and families who now live far from Kashmir still try to come back to the spring for it, carrying milk and pudding the way their grandparents did. A temple can be a place you visit. This one is also a mother's house you return to.

segments.voice: A kitchen in winter. On a clean cloth, a row of pots, filled to the brim with water, and in the water, walnuts, still in their shells. Someone has drawn on the pots and hung flowers around their necks. The family will sit up with them tonight, singing, worshiping, keeping the lamp going. In a day or two, those walnuts will be soft from the water and on their way to every relative and neighbor on the list. This is Herath, Shiva's great night, kept the Kashmiri way, and the last of the Kashmir days.
screen: `POTS OF WATER AND WALNUTS` → `A NIGHT KEPT AWAKE` → `HERATH`

segments.voice: You met Mahashivaratri in year one: the great night of Shiva, kept with fasting and worship and staying awake. Kashmiri Pandits keep it too, and they call it Herath. In their tradition it's a night kept at home, around the family, more than at a temple. The family sets out a pot and smaller vessels, filled with water and walnuts, and calls the arrangement the vatuk. It's worshiped as Shiva and the company around him. Families tell the meaning in different ways. Some speak of Shiva's wedding to Parvati, with the pots as the wedding guests. Others speak of Bhairava, a fierce form of Shiva, appearing as light. Nobody has to settle it tonight. When the worship is over, the soaked walnuts become prasad, and here's the teaching. Prasad means grace: what was offered to God comes back blessed, and grace isn't meant to be kept on a shelf. It's handed on. So the walnuts go out: to grandparents, to cousins, to the family next door. In the days after, people visit each other with greetings. The night that begins alone with God ends at other people's doors. It's the same reason a Hindu friend presses a sweet into your hand after a puja, and why it's polite to take it with your right hand and say thank you. And that closes the week: from Pandharpur's spire to Kashmir's lake, its kings, a theater, a recognition, a spring, and last, a holy night with a kitchen at its center.
